stem: A team tunes a support-bot prompt by eyeballing a handful of chats, and each fix seems to break some other case. What should they do first?

choices.text: Hand-grade ten ideal conversations in depth before and after every single prompt change
choices.reason: The guidance prioritizes volume: more automatically graded questions beat fewer high-quality hand-graded ones.

choices.text: Build a test set from only typical, well-formed customer messages, leaving out unusual inputs
choices.reason: Evals should mirror the real task distribution, and the guidance says not to forget edge cases.

choices.text: Define success criteria, then build an auto-graded, task-specific eval set with edge cases
choices.reason: Correct: defining success criteria and designing evaluations to measure against them is the cycle central to prompt engineering.

choices.text: Keep rewording the prompt until the same handful of chats all look right to the team
choices.reason: A few eyeballed chats don't mirror the real task distribution, so you can't tell whether a change helped overall.

takeaway: Measure, don't eyeball: set **success criteria**, then build an **automated, task-specific** eval set that includes edge cases.
explanation: Each fix breaking another case shows the team can't measure whether a change helps overall. The central cycle is to define success criteria, then design evaluations to measure against them: an automated, task-specific set that mirrors real inputs, edge cases included (C). Option A is the tempting trap, since careful hand-grading feels rigorous, but the guidance favors volume of automatically graded questions. Option B leaves out edge cases, and D keeps eyeballing the same few chats.
mnemonic: Criteria first, then many automated tests.

source.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: Your app on Claude Opus 5.5 retries failed requests. One request returns HTTP 200 with `stop_reason: "refusal"` and empty content. Your handler re-sends it unchanged to the same model, which refuses again. What's the better recovery?

choices.text: Keep retrying on the same model with exponential backoff until a request finally succeeds
choices.reason: A refusal is a normal response, not an error, and re-sending a refused request to the same model usually earns another refusal.

choices.text: Re-send it on a fallback model, or let server-side fallback (`fallbacks`) retry it
choices.reason: Correct: you can usually still get an answer by sending the same request to another Claude model; server-side fallback (beta) does this in one API call.

choices.text: Parse the `stop_details.explanation` text to decide whether the request is worth retrying
choices.reason: The explanation text isn't stable, so display it rather than parse it; branch on `stop_reason` equal to `"refusal"`.

choices.text: Record it as a 5xx error so that your existing error-rate alerts fire on refusals
choices.reason: A refusal is an HTTP 200, so monitoring built on error rates or 5xx never sees it. Instrument refusals as their own signal.

takeaway: A refusal is a **model-output** outcome, not a transient error: retry on a **different model**, not the same one.
explanation: A refusal is a normal HTTP 200 **model output**, not a transient error, so re-sending it unchanged to the same model usually earns another refusal. The better recovery is sending the same request to another Claude model, or using server-side fallback (`fallbacks`, beta) to do it in one call (B). Option A is the trap, treating it like a retryable failure. Option C parses `stop_details.explanation`, which isn't stable, and D mislabels a 200 as a 5xx.
mnemonic: Refused? Change the model, not the timing.

diagram.caption: Another Claude model can usually serve a refused request.

stem: After you move your agent to a newer Claude model, a tool handler that compares the tool input's raw JSON text with an expected string starts failing, even though the values look the same when printed. What should you change?

choices.text: Parse the input with `JSON.parse()` or `json.loads()`, then compare the values
choices.reason: Correct: Unicode and forward-slash escaping differs between model versions, so parse the input and never do raw string matching on serialized input.

choices.text: Add `strict: true` to the tool definition so that values are escaped consistently
choices.reason: Strict mode addresses invented parameters and wrong parameter types, not how the same values are escaped.

choices.text: Sharpen the tool's description so that Claude sends the exact expected string
choices.reason: Sharper descriptions fix Claude calling the wrong tool; here the right tool is called with the right values.

choices.text: Add `input_examples` that show the exact expected string for that parameter
choices.reason: `input_examples` help when Claude never calls a tool or picks values outside your enum; for escaping differences, the fix is to parse the JSON.

takeaway: Compare **parsed** tool inputs, never serialized strings: escaping can differ between model versions.
explanation: The values print the same but the **raw JSON text** differs, because Unicode and forward-slash escaping can differ between model versions. The fix is to parse the input with `JSON.parse()` or `json.loads()` and compare values, never serialized strings (A). Option B is the tempting trap: `strict: true` sounds like it enforces consistency, but it addresses invented parameters and wrong types, not escaping. Options C and D fix tool selection and value choice, neither of which is wrong here.

stem: You use Claude to grade 2,000 support replies for helpfulness. The grader writes paragraphs of free-form commentary that are hard to aggregate, and similar replies get different verdicts. Which change follows Anthropic's tips for LLM-based grading?

choices.text: Switch to human grading for all 2,000 replies, so that every single verdict is consistent
choices.reason: Human grading is the most flexible and high quality, but slow and expensive; the guidance says to avoid it if possible.

choices.text: Grade by exact string match against one golden reply written for each support ticket
choices.reason: Code-based grading is fast and reliable, but lacks nuance for complex judgments like helpfulness.

choices.text: Ask the grader for a numeric score only, with no reasoning or thinking, to keep it fast
choices.reason: The tips say to use a grader with thinking on, so it reasons before it scores; this improves performance, particularly on tasks requiring complex judgment.

choices.text: Give a detailed rubric, turn thinking on, and ask for only "correct"/"incorrect" or 1–5
choices.reason: Correct: use detailed, clear rubrics, an empirical or specific output (purely qualitative evaluations are hard to assess at scale) and a grader with thinking on.

takeaway: An LLM grader needs a **clear rubric**, a **specific output** and thinking on; test its reliability before you scale.
explanation: Two symptoms point to the fix: free-form commentary is hard to aggregate, and similar replies get different verdicts. Anthropic's tips are a detailed rubric, a specific output such as 'correct'/'incorrect' or 1–5, and a grader with thinking on (D). Option C is the tempting half-fix: a numeric-only score aggregates well, but turning thinking off loses the reasoning that improves complex judgments. Option A is slow and expensive human grading, and B's exact match lacks the nuance helpfulness needs.

source.title: Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: An Agent SDK agent sometimes takes minutes on simple tasks, and you're exporting its OpenTelemetry traces. How should you use the traces to find where the time goes?

choices.text: Compare the model-request and tool spans under each interaction to spot the slow step
choices.reason: Correct: each turn is an interaction span, with child spans for every model request (with latency) and every tool call, so the slow step stands out.

choices.text: Use metrics alone, since traces record only the agent's final answer
choices.reason: Traces hold a span for each interaction, model request, tool call and hook; they are the most detailed view of a run.

choices.text: Compare total token counts, which show which step took longest
choices.reason: Token counts measure spend, not where the time went; per-step latency is on the request and tool spans.

choices.text: Set the trace exporter to `console` and read it in the SDK's message stream
choices.reason: The console exporter writes to standard output, which the SDK uses as its message channel; don't use it with the SDK.

takeaway: To find a slow step, read the **trace**: model-request and tool spans nest under each interaction.
explanation: Trace analysis locates a failure or slowdown step by step: every model request and tool call is its own span under the turn's interaction span, so the slow one is visible (A). Traces record far more than the final answer (B), token totals don't show time (C), and the console exporter would corrupt the SDK's message channel (D).

stem: Your tool-using agent with thinking worked until you changed the loop to drop `thinking` blocks from each assistant message before appending the `tool_result`, to save tokens. Now every follow-up request fails with 400 `invalid_request_error`, and retrying doesn't help. What's the cause?

choices.text: The API is overloaded; retry with a longer backoff
choices.reason: Overload is `529 overloaded_error`. A 400 means an issue with the format or content of your request, which a retry sends again unchanged.

choices.text: Your API key lacks access to thinking; rotate it
choices.reason: Key problems show up as `401 authentication_error` or `403 permission_error`, not as a 400 about your request.

choices.text: Your thinking config is outdated; switch to `thinking: {"type": "enabled"}`
choices.reason: The same thinking config worked before the loop change, so it isn't the cause; on Claude 4.7 and later models, `enabled` itself returns a 400.

choices.text: Your loop dropped the thinking blocks; pass them back exactly as received
choices.reason: Correct: edited, reordered, filtered-out or reconstructed thinking blocks in the latest assistant message return a 400; pass every `thinking` and `redacted_thinking` block back.

takeaway: A 400 after a code change is an **integration** bug: fix what your request sends instead of retrying it.
explanation: The break started right after a **code change**, and the error is a 400 that retries don't fix, which points at your request. Edited, filtered-out or reconstructed thinking blocks in the latest assistant message return a 400, so pass every `thinking` and `redacted_thinking` block back exactly as received (D). Option C is the tempting trap, blaming the config, but that same config worked before the loop change. Option A would be a 529, and B a 401 or 403.

stem: Your agent loop sends each tool's output as a `tool_result` block followed by a text block saying "Here are the results." Claude increasingly replies with an empty response and `stop_reason: "end_turn"`. Whose fault is this, and what's the fix?

choices.text: The model's: re-send the empty response unchanged until Claude produces some text
choices.reason: Sending the empty response back won't help: Claude already determined it's done, so it will remain done.

choices.text: The model's: raise `max_tokens`, because the turn ended before Claude could answer
choices.reason: A response cut off by your limit has `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`; these turns ended with `end_turn`.

choices.text: Yours: drop the text after the `tool_result` blocks and send only the results
choices.reason: Correct: text right after tool results teaches Claude to expect user input after every tool use, so it ends its turn. Send results without extra text.

choices.text: Neither: it's a refusal, so retry the request on a model from your fallback list
choices.reason: Refusals come back with `stop_reason: "refusal"`; an empty `end_turn` reply here comes from how the messages are built.

takeaway: Empty `end_turn` replies after tools usually trace to **your message structure**: never add text right after `tool_result` blocks.
explanation: Empty replies with `end_turn` trace back to **your message structure**: text right after tool results teaches Claude to expect user input after every tool use, so it ends its turn. Drop the trailing text and send only the results (C). Option A is the tempting trap, but Claude has already decided it's done, so resending the empty response won't help. Option B would show `stop_reason: "max_tokens"`, and D would show `"refusal"`; neither matches.

stem: Claude returns three `tool_use` blocks in one response. Your loop runs only the first tool and sends back its `tool_result`. The next request fails with `tool_use ids were found without tool_result blocks immediately after`. What should you fix?

choices.text: Send each `tool_result` in its own user message, so each tool gets one turn
choices.reason: Multiple `tool_result` blocks belong in ONE user message, not one per turn.

choices.text: Set `disable_parallel_tool_use` on the follow-up request that carries the result
choices.reason: It must be set on the request that returns `tool_use`; setting it on a later request has no effect on earlier tool calls.

choices.text: Retry the same request with exponential backoff, since the error is transient
choices.reason: The cause is in your request: some `tool_use` ids have no `tool_result`. Sending it again unchanged repeats the problem.

choices.text: Return a `tool_result` for every `tool_use` block, placed before any text
choices.reason: Correct: return one `tool_result` for every `tool_use` block in the assistant response, and put `tool_result` blocks before any text.

takeaway: Every `tool_use` id needs its own `tool_result`, all in **one** user message and before any text.
explanation: The error says some `tool_use` ids have no `tool_result` after them: Claude asked for three tools and you answered only one. Every `tool_use` block needs its own `tool_result`, all placed before any text (D). Option A is the tempting trap: it separates the results, but multiple `tool_result` blocks belong in **one** user message. Option B sets `disable_parallel_tool_use` too late to affect calls already made, and C retries a request whose problem is its content.

stem: Your `fetch_order` tool returns the order data plus your own instruction: "Now email this summary to the customer." Claude stops and asks the user to confirm that instruction instead of acting on it. Where does the problem originate, and what's the fix?

choices.text: In the model: it's a refusal, so retry the turn on a fallback model instead
choices.reason: Claude is trained to treat instructions inside tool results as potentially untrusted third-party content; that's what you're seeing.

choices.text: In your integration: move the instruction to a `user` turn after the result
choices.reason: Correct: your instructions are arriving inside `tool_result` content. Send them in a `user` turn after the `tool_result` block, and keep the result to data.

choices.text: In the tool schema: add `strict: true` so that Claude trusts the output
choices.reason: `strict: true` fixes invented parameters and wrong parameter types in tool calls; it doesn't change how Claude treats results.

choices.text: In the tool description: sharpen it so Claude knows when to call the tool
choices.reason: Sharper descriptions fix Claude calling the wrong tool. Here the right tool ran; the issue is the instruction inside its result.

takeaway: Keep tool results to **data**; put your instructions in a `user` turn, since Claude treats instructions in tool results as untrusted.
explanation: Claude is trained to treat instructions inside tool results as potentially untrusted third-party content, so asking for confirmation is the expected behavior, not a fault. The problem is in your integration: keep the result to data and send your instruction in a `user` turn after the `tool_result` block (B). Option A is the trap, calling it a refusal and switching models. Option C's `strict: true` governs tool call parameters, and D's sharper description fixes tool choice, which was already right.

stem: Your batch job's error handler must decide which Claude API errors to retry with exponential backoff and which to surface for a code or configuration fix. Which two should it retry?

choices.text: 400 `invalid_request_error`
choices.reason: There was an issue with the format or content of your request; fix the request rather than resend it.

choices.text: 500 `api_error`
choices.reason: Correct: an unexpected internal error. Retry with exponential backoff, and contact support with the request ID if it persists.

choices.text: 401 `authentication_error`
choices.reason: There's an issue with your API key (for example, it's malformed, revoked or expired), so fix the key.

choices.text: 413 `request_too_large`
choices.reason: The request exceeds the maximum allowed bytes (32 MB for Messages); resending it won't make it smaller.

choices.text: 529 `overloaded_error`
choices.reason: Correct: the API is temporarily overloaded. Like other 5xx failures, the SDK retries it with backoff by default.

takeaway: Retry **transient** failures (500, 529, connection errors) with backoff; 400, 401 and 413 need a fix, not a retry.
explanation: The split is **transient versus fixable**. 500 `api_error` is an unexpected internal error (B) and 529 `overloaded_error` means temporary overload (E); both are worth retrying with exponential backoff. Option D is the most tempting wrong pick, since size can feel like a passing problem, but a request over the limit is still too large however often you resend it. Option A is a request-format problem and C is a bad API key, so both need a fix, not a retry.

stem: In an agent's trace, one `claude_code.tool` span lasts 90 seconds. Its permission-wait child span accounts for almost all of that time, and its execution child span is short. Where is the delay?

choices.text: Inside the tool's own code, which needs to be optimized
choices.reason: The execution child span, which wraps the tool actually running, is the short one.

choices.text: In the model request that decided to call the tool
choices.reason: Model requests have their own `claude_code.llm_request` spans; they aren't inside the tool span.

choices.text: Waiting for the tool call to be approved, not running the tool
choices.reason: Correct: a tool span has separate child spans for the permission wait and for the execution, and here the wait dominates.

choices.text: In a hook that runs inside every tool span
choices.reason: Hooks get their own `claude_code.hook` spans, separate from a tool's permission-wait and execution children.

takeaway: Read a tool span's children: **permission wait** versus **execution** tells you whether to fix approvals or code.
explanation: Each tool span splits into a permission-wait child and an execution child. Here almost all the time is the wait, so the delay is approval, not the tool (C). The execution span is short (A), model requests and hooks have their own spans outside this breakdown (B, D), so they can't explain this tool span's time.

stem: Your `search_orders` tool wrapper turns Claude's tool input into a database query string, and a bug in how it formats dates reached production. You want the cheapest test that checks this one function on its own, on every change. What should you write?

choices.text: An end-to-end test that asks the chat app about last week's orders and checks the reply
choices.reason: A full-system run exercises everything, and bringing a system up with its dependencies can take minutes to hours. It also doesn't isolate the wrapper.

choices.text: A unit test that calls the wrapper directly with sample inputs and checks the query it builds
choices.reason: Correct: a unit test is the smallest and simplest form of test. It checks one separable piece, such as a function, on its own and usually runs in milliseconds.

choices.text: An integration test that runs the wrapper against the real database with the model in the loop
choices.reason: Integration tests verify that an assembled component works correctly. They cost more and aren't the cheapest way to check one function's own logic.

choices.text: A smoke test that starts the whole system and checks that one critical request succeeds
choices.reason: Smoke tests are simple system tests of critical behavior. They need the whole system running and don't target the date-formatting logic.

takeaway: One function, checked on its own and fast: that's a **unit test**. Parsers and tool wrappers are the classic targets.
explanation: A unit test checks one separable piece, such as a function, in isolation, and it usually finishes in milliseconds, which makes it cheap enough to run on every change. The deciding detail is that the bug sits inside one function, the tool wrapper. Choice a is tempting because a full run would eventually hit the bug, but it's slow, costly and doesn't point at the wrapper.

stem: A test sends one support email to Claude and expects back JSON with `name`, `email` and `plan` fields. You can't predict the exact values Claude will write. Which check makes this test both stable and useful?

choices.text: Check that the API returned HTTP 200, since a successful call means the reply is usable
choices.reason: A refusal also comes back with a 200 status code, and its output may not match your schema, so a 200 alone doesn't prove the reply's shape.

choices.text: Check that the words name, email and plan each appear somewhere in the reply text
choices.reason: Word matching misses the real failures: invalid JSON syntax, missing required fields and inconsistent data types.

choices.text: Parse the reply as JSON and check each required field is there with the right type
choices.reason: Correct: this checks the shape downstream code relies on, catching parse errors, missing required fields and inconsistent data types.

choices.text: Retry the call until the reply parses, then mark the test as passed on that attempt
choices.reason: Schema violations that need retries are exactly the failure to catch; passing on a later attempt hides it.

takeaway: Test one Claude call by its **shape**: it parses, the required fields are there, and the types are right.
explanation: When you can't predict the exact text, a stable test checks what must hold on every run: the reply is valid JSON with the required fields and types. That catches the failures that break downstream code. Choice a is tempting because a 200 looks like success, but a refusal also returns 200 with output that may not match the schema.

stem: A test asserts that Claude's summary of a fixed article exactly equals a summary saved last week. With no change to the code or the prompt, it passes on one run and fails on the next. What explains this, and what should the test check instead?

choices.text: The article is cached between runs, so clear the cache to give every run identical input
choices.reason: Nothing about the input changed between runs. Identical inputs can still produce different outputs across API calls.

choices.text: Temperature 0 makes the output identical every time, so keep the exact-match check
choices.reason: Even with temperature set to 0, results aren't fully deterministic, so an exact-text assertion stays flaky.

choices.text: A third-party cloud provider adds the variation, so call Anthropic's own API directly
choices.reason: Non-determinism applies both to Anthropic's first-party service and to inference through third-party cloud providers.

choices.text: The same input can vary in output, so check properties of the summary, not its text
choices.reason: Correct: identical inputs may produce different outputs across API calls, so a stable test checks what must hold every time, not the exact wording.

takeaway: Claude's wording varies run to run, so assert **shape and properties**, never exact text.
explanation: Model output is non-deterministic: the same input can come back worded differently on the next call, even at temperature 0. A test that compares exact text will flake with no code change. Choice b is tempting because lowering temperature makes output more conservative, but it doesn't make it fully deterministic.

stem: In your RAG app, the retrieval function passes its unit tests, and so does the function that builds the prompt. Yet the model never sees the retrieved passages: retrieval returns objects, and the prompt builder expects plain strings. Which test would catch this?

choices.text: An integration test that feeds retrieval's real result into the prompt builder
choices.reason: Correct: an integration test runs on assembled components to verify they work correctly together. This bug lives in the handoff, which no unit test exercises.

choices.text: More unit tests for retrieval, covering a wider range of queries and empty results
choices.reason: A unit test checks one piece on its own. Retrieval already works by itself, so more unit tests never touch the handoff.

choices.text: A test of one model call with hand-written context, checking the reply's fields
choices.reason: Hand-writing the context skips the retrieval step, so the mismatch between the two components never appears.

choices.text: A regression test that replays last month's fixed bugs against the prompt builder
choices.reason: Regression tests stop previously fixed bugs from coming back. This is a new bug in how two components connect.

takeaway: Every piece can pass alone while the **handoff** between them is broken; only an **integration test** crosses it.
explanation: Unit tests check each piece in isolation, so two components can both pass while disagreeing about the data they exchange. An integration test assembles the pieces and checks they work together, which is where this bug lives. Choice c is tempting because it tests a model call, but writing the context by hand bypasses retrieval entirely.

diagram.caption: Each piece passes alone; the integration test covers the handoff between them.

stem: Every unit and integration test for your chat assistant passes. After release, users who type a question into the web app never see an answer, because the page posts to an outdated backend route. What kind of test would have caught this before release?

choices.text: A unit test for the function that formats Claude's reply before it's displayed
choices.reason: That function can work perfectly. The bug is in how the whole flow is wired, which a test of one function never runs.

choices.text: An end-to-end test that submits a question in the web app and checks for an answer
choices.reason: Correct: an end-to-end test runs the whole flow as a user would, from input to output, so a broken route anywhere along it shows up.

choices.text: An integration test of the handoff from the retrieval step into the model call
choices.reason: That handoff isn't where the failure is. An integration test covers one connection, not the page-to-backend path a user takes.

choices.text: A larger eval set of prompts sent directly to the model to grade answer quality
choices.reason: Calling the model directly skips the web app and the backend route, so it can't see a wiring failure between them.

takeaway: Only an **end-to-end test** runs the flow the way a user does, so it catches wiring that smaller tests never reach.
explanation: The largest-scale test checks the system's end-to-end functionality, from the user's input to the output they see. Here every piece works and the failure is in how the page connects to the backend, so only a full run reaches it. Choice d is tempting because evals feel thorough, but sending prompts straight to the model skips the broken route.

stem: Your team's only tests are end-to-end runs of the whole agent. A run takes about an hour, and when one fails nobody can tell which part broke. Which two additions address this?

choices.text: Unit tests for pieces such as the output parser and each tool wrapper
choices.reason: Correct: unit tests check one separable piece on its own and usually finish in milliseconds, so a failure points straight at that piece.

choices.text: More end-to-end cases, so that every feature is covered by at least one full run
choices.reason: More full runs add runtime and still don't show which part broke when one fails.

choices.text: Rerunning each failed end-to-end test until it passes before reporting it
choices.reason: Rerunning until a pass hides failures instead of locating them, and it adds the cost of more full runs.

choices.text: Integration tests for handoffs, such as a retrieval result passed into the model call
choices.reason: Correct: an integration test verifies that an assembled component works, so a failure narrows to that connection without running the whole system.

choices.text: Dropping the end-to-end tests, since smaller tests can catch every failure they find
choices.reason: Only the largest-scale test checks the system's end-to-end functionality. Smaller tests complement it; they don't replace it.

takeaway: Smaller tests make failures **cheap to find and easy to place**; keep the end-to-end run for what only it can see.
explanation: An end-to-end run tells you the flow failed, not where, and it's slow. Unit tests isolate single functions and integration tests isolate single handoffs, so a failure in either points at one place and runs fast. Choice e is tempting once smaller tests exist, but the whole-system check still catches failures they can't reach.

stem: An agent that searches, calls two tools and then answers gives a wrong final answer on one eval case. Your logs record only the user's input and the final reply. What would let you see which step produced the bad result?

choices.text: Run the failing case ten more times and keep whichever answer appears most often
choices.reason: Rerunning shows how often the case fails, not where. You still can't see any step between the input and the output.

choices.text: Log the whole request's total token count and latency alongside the input
choices.reason: Totals for the whole request don't separate the steps. A trace breaks a request into spans, one per model request or tool use.

choices.text: Trace the run, so each model request and tool use is recorded as its own step
choices.reason: Correct: a trace is the full record of one request through your system, and each span is one step; traces are meant for debugging failed or slow requests.

choices.text: Add the failing case to an end-to-end suite so it's caught before each release
choices.reason: That catches the failure again but still records only input and output, so it doesn't show which step went wrong.

takeaway: A test tells you **that** a case failed; a **trace** tells you **which step** failed.
explanation: Input-and-output logs show the symptom but hide everything in between. A trace records each step of the run as its own span, such as each model request and tool use, so you can see where the bad result first appeared. Choice d is tempting because more coverage feels useful, but catching the failure again doesn't explain it.

stem: A RAG assistant gave a wrong answer. In the trace, the retrieval step returned three passages, none containing the answer, and the model request's input shows those same passages. The model's response sticks to what it was given. Where should you start fixing?

choices.text: The prompt's wording, since the model should have known the right answer anyway
choices.reason: The trace shows the model answered from the context it was given, and that context lacked the answer, so the prompt isn't the first suspect.

choices.text: The model choice, since a more capable model would have found the missing fact
choices.reason: The bad result was already in the retrieval step's output, before any model saw it; the trace points upstream of the model.

choices.text: The response parser, since the reply must have changed after the model returned it
choices.reason: The trace shows the model's response matched the context it received; nothing points at a step after the model request.

choices.text: The retrieval step, since the right passage never made it into the model's input
choices.reason: Correct: reading the steps in order, the first bad output came from retrieval, so that is where the failure originated.

takeaway: Follow the trace to the **first step whose output is wrong**; that's where the problem began, not where it surfaced.
explanation: A trace lets you check each step's input and output in order. Here the model faithfully used what it received, and what it received was already missing the answer, so the problem began at retrieval. Choice a is tempting because the wrong answer came out of the model, but the model wasn't where things first went wrong.

diagram.caption: The first wrong output is where the failure began.

stem: Some users see "No answer available". For those requests, the trace shows the model request returned a correct, well-formed answer, but your application's span right after it records an error while reading that response. Where is the problem?

choices.text: In your code that handles the model's response, not in the model's output itself
choices.reason: Correct: the model's step produced a good result, and the first bad result is your own code reading it, so the fix is in the integration layer.

choices.text: In the model's output, so the prompt needs examples of the expected answer format
choices.reason: The trace shows the response was correct and well formed; changing the prompt won't fix code that mishandles it.

choices.text: In the retrieval step, because the model must have answered from missing context
choices.reason: The model's answer was correct, so its context was fine; the failure first appears in the step after the model's good response.

choices.text: In the API itself, so wrap every model request in retries with exponential backoff
choices.reason: The model request succeeded and returned a correct answer; retrying it repeats a step that already worked.

takeaway: Good model output followed by an error in your span means an **integration-layer** bug; don't touch the prompt.
explanation: Traces show each request inside your application's own spans, so you can see the model's step and your code's step side by side. Here the model returned a correct answer and the error starts in your code reading it, which places the bug in the integration layer. Choice b is tempting because users see a bad answer, but the model's output was fine.

stem: Your agent sometimes takes minutes to answer a simple question. Your logs record only the total time of each request, so you can't tell where the time goes. What would show you which step is slow?

choices.text: Switch to a faster model, then compare the new total time with the old one
choices.reason: That guesses at the cause. The total time still won't show whether the delay is in a model request or in a tool use.

choices.text: Trace the requests, so each model request and tool use is a span with its timing
choices.reason: Correct: a trace breaks one request into spans, one per step such as a model request or a tool use, and traces are meant for debugging failed or slow requests.

choices.text: Add an end-to-end test that fails whenever the total response time is too long
choices.reason: That flags slow runs again, but it measures the same total time, so it still doesn't show which step is slow.

choices.text: Raise the request timeout so that slow requests can finish instead of failing
choices.reason: A longer timeout hides the symptom. It records nothing about where the time went.

takeaway: Slow or failing run? A **trace** times each step separately, so you can see which one is the problem.
explanation: A total time per request shows that a run is slow, not where. A trace records each step, such as each model request and tool use, as its own span with its own timing, which is why traces are used to debug failed or slow requests. Choice a is tempting because a faster model often helps, but if the delay is in a tool it changes nothing, and you still can't see why.

stem: Your agent test checks that the agent calls `lookup_customer`, then `check_inventory`, then `create_order`, in exactly that order. A new version checks inventory first, creates the correct order, and fails the test. What does Anthropic's guidance on agent evals suggest?

choices.text: Keep the exact-sequence check, because any change in tool order signals a regression
choices.reason: Agents regularly find valid approaches that eval designers didn't anticipate; failing them punishes creativity, not mistakes.

choices.text: Compare the agent's final reply text with the reply the previous version gave
choices.reason: Model outputs vary between runs, so matching the reply text is brittle; check the outcome, such as whether the order exists.

choices.text: Grade what the agent produced, such as whether the correct order now exists
choices.reason: Correct: it's often better to grade what the agent produced, not the path it took. The outcome is the final state, like a record that really exists.

choices.text: Fix the tool order in the system prompt so that every run follows the same path
choices.reason: The guidance is to stop grading the path, not to force one; agents often find valid approaches designers didn't anticipate.

takeaway: Test an agent by its **outcome**, not by the exact steps it took to get there.
explanation: Agents often reach the right result by a route nobody planned for, so a test that demands one exact sequence fails good runs. Grading the outcome, such as whether the order now exists, keeps the test focused on what matters. Choice a is tempting because a changed sequence looks like a regression, but here the result was correct.

stem: Your support bot's suite has two kinds of checks: code checks (the reply parses, required fields exist, the right tool was called) and a model-graded rubric for tone. You want to keep grading costs down without losing coverage. How should you split the work?

choices.text: Use code checks wherever they can decide the result, and the model grader only for tone
choices.reason: Correct: Anthropic recommends deterministic graders where possible and LLM graders where necessary. Code graders are fast and cheap; model graders cost more.

choices.text: Send every check to the model grader so that all results come from one consistent judge
choices.reason: Model graders are non-deterministic and more expensive than code, so using them where code can decide adds cost without benefit.

choices.text: Use code checks for tone as well, matching each reply against a list of approved phrases
choices.reason: Code graders are brittle to valid variations and lack nuance, so they handle subjective qualities such as tone poorly.

choices.text: Replace both with a human reviewer who reads a sample of replies after every change
choices.reason: Manual review is time-intensive and doesn't scale; systematic human review is best kept for calibrating model graders or subjective outputs.

takeaway: Route each check to the cheapest grader that can decide it: **code where possible, a model where necessary**.
explanation: Code graders are fast, cheap and reproducible, so they should decide everything they can, like whether the reply parses or the right tool was called. A model grader earns its higher cost only on judgment calls such as tone. Choice b is tempting because one judge sounds consistent, but model graders are themselves non-deterministic and cost more.

stem: Your full end-to-end suite calls the live model, takes about an hour and costs money on every run. Many broken builds fail on something basic, such as the service not starting at all. How can you avoid paying for the full run on those builds?

choices.text: Run the full suite on every build, but on a random half of its cases
choices.reason: That still pays for a long run on every broken build, and it drops coverage on the builds that work.

choices.text: Run the full suite twice on each build and keep the better of the two results
choices.reason: That doubles the cost of every run, including the broken builds you wanted to stop early.

choices.text: Replace the end-to-end suite with unit tests, since they catch the same failures
choices.reason: Unit tests check pieces in isolation; only a system-level test checks the system's end-to-end functionality.

choices.text: Run a quick smoke test first, and start the full suite only if it passes
choices.reason: Correct: smoke tests check very simple but critical behavior, and they serve to short-circuit additional and more expensive testing.

takeaway: Let a cheap **smoke test** gate the expensive run, so you pay for the full suite only on builds worth testing.
explanation: A smoke test checks very simple but critical behavior, such as whether the service starts and answers one request. If it fails, there's no point paying for the hour-long run. Choice c is tempting because unit tests are cheap, but they test pieces in isolation and can't replace a whole-system check.

diagram.caption: Cheap checks run first and stop broken builds before the expensive run.

stem: One case in your agent eval passes on some runs and fails on others, with no change to the agent. A teammate wants to delete it as flaky. What does Anthropic's eval guidance suggest instead?

choices.text: Delete it, because a case that doesn't give the same result every run gives no signal
choices.reason: Model outputs vary between runs by nature; that's handled by running multiple trials, not by dropping cases.

choices.text: Keep only the first run's result so that the eval stays fast and reproducible
choices.reason: One run of a varying output is a single sample; running multiple trials produces more consistent results.

choices.text: Run several trials of the case and read the transcripts of the ones that fail
choices.reason: Correct: because outputs vary between runs, run multiple trials; the transcript shows whether the agent erred or the grader rejected a valid answer.

choices.text: Lower the grader's pass threshold until the case passes on every single run
choices.reason: That hides real failures; the transcript tells you whether the agent made a genuine mistake or the grader rejected a valid solution.

takeaway: A case that passes only sometimes needs **multiple trials and a look at the transcripts**, not deletion.
explanation: Because model outputs vary between runs, one run is only a sample; multiple trials show how often the case really fails. Reading the transcripts of the failures then tells you whether the agent made a mistake or the grader was wrong. Choice a is tempting because flaky tests are usually removed, but here the variation is expected and still carries signal.

stem: Users report that your research agent sometimes misses obvious information, and rerunning their queries doesn't reproduce it. You can't see why it happens. Which two practices help you find the cause?

choices.text: Rerun the exact prompt until the bug reproduces, since the same input gives the same run
choices.reason: Agents make dynamic decisions and are non-deterministic between runs, even with identical prompts.

choices.text: Add full production tracing so that you can diagnose why the agent failed
choices.reason: Correct: Anthropic added full production tracing, which let them diagnose why agents failed and fix issues systematically.

choices.text: Add more unit tests for each tool, since the misses must come from a tool bug
choices.reason: That assumes the cause before you can see it. A miss could come from poor search queries, weak sources or tool failures; tracing shows which.

choices.text: Wait until enough user reports pile up for the pattern to show on its own
choices.reason: The reports said the agent wasn't finding obvious information but couldn't show why; seeing why took tracing.

choices.text: Monitor the agent's decision patterns and how its parts interact
choices.reason: Correct: Anthropic monitored agent decision patterns and interaction structures, without reading individual conversations, to find root causes and fix common failures.

takeaway: When an agent fails in ways you can't reproduce, **production tracing** of its decisions shows you why.
explanation: Agents are non-deterministic, so a reported failure often won't recur on a rerun, and user reports describe what went wrong but not why. For its multi-agent research system, Anthropic added full production tracing plus monitoring of decision patterns and interaction structures, without reading conversation contents. Choice a is tempting because rerunning is the usual way to reproduce a bug, but identical prompts don't guarantee identical runs.
